output.title: Treat data cleaning as a workflow boundary, not a feature
output.body:
If you run a small business, data cleaning is usually not the real decision. The real decision is whether a recurring workflow only works if the input data is clean enough to trust. That is a design constraint, not a tool choice.

Think about invoices, customer records, or form replies. If they arrive in a predictable format, you can write down the rule that matters before anything downstream happens. If the inputs are messy and you cannot state the success rule in plain English, AI is probably the wrong place to start. Manual cleaning, or no automation at all, may be the more honest option. Fancy software is not a substitute for a missing rulebook.

That is the same way we think about control in the self-built demos. The knowledge assistant works only with approved material, and the accounts-payable demo uses checks plus human-only approval on synthetic data. Those are working examples of control, not customer deployments.

Bareni’s diagnostic is simple: name the one recurring workflow, describe the input structure, and write the quality rule that matters. For example, an owner might say: invoice amount, supplier, and reference must match before a human approves anything. That is a useful boundary. The human still approves the decision, especially where money or other high-risk work is involved.

One practical next step: take one repeated workflow and ask, “Does this happen the same way every week, and can I write the quality rules in plain English?”
